Mastery of these tools speeds up every task that follows, whether you are placing a cube, positioning a camera, or building a level. A common beginner mistake is to ignore the Project organization and Inspector details; this leads to confusion as a project grows. As you listen, imagine creating a new project, placing a cube, and saving a scene. Keep an eye out for the practical checks and a small hands-on activity that shows how these pieces connect. By the end you'll have a clear mental map of the editor and a small routine to keep your work safe and organized.

screens.title: The Unity Editor: the central workspace
screens.narratorSegment: The Unity Editor is an integrated development environment composed of several specialized windows that each play a unique role in building a game. The Scene view is your interactive 3D canvas where you place, move, and arrange GameObjects such as characters, lights, and props. The Game view shows the rendered output from the active camera and simulates what a player will see during runtime. The Hierarchy lists every GameObject in the current scene and reveals parent-child relationships you can use to group and transform objects together. The Project window is your project's asset repository: models, textures, audio, scripts, and saved scenes live here whether or not they are in the current scene. Finally, the Inspector displays editable properties and components for whatever you have selected, giving you precise control over transform values, material settings, and script variables. A helpful way to remember their roles is to treat the Project as your toolbox, the Hierarchy as the parts list for this scene, the Scene as the assembly table, the Inspector as the fine-tuner, and the Game view as the test bench. A common misconception is to confuse Scene and Game: editing happens in Scene, while Game shows runtime output. Practice by selecting a default cube, noticing how the Inspector updates, and dragging an asset from the Project into the Scene so it appears in the Hierarchy. That small loop demonstrates how the windows interact and why understanding them speeds every stage of development.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Core Concept
Windows and their purpose
Define each window and see how a small asset moves through the editor workflow.
Scene view
Interactive 3D workspace for placing GameObjects and composing levels.
Game view
Runtime preview using the active camera—what players will see.
Hierarchy & Project
Hierarchy lists objects in scene; Project stores assets across the project.
Inspector
Edit Transform, materials, and component values for the selected object.
Workflow example
Drag a model from the Project window into the Scene. It appears in the Scene view and is listed in the Hierarchy. Click the object and use the Inspector to adjust position, rotation, and scale. Press Play to check the Game view and confirm how a player perceives the object.
Concrete example
Import a model, drag it into the Scene, then select it and change its Transform values in the Inspector to move it above the ground plane.
Common mistake
Confusing Scene editing with Game preview leads to changing objects that look right in Scene but are off-axis in the player camera. Always check Game view before finalizing placement.
Key Takeaway

Each window serves a distinct role; understanding the flow—Project → Scene → Hierarchy → Inspector → Game—makes editing faster and less error-prone.

screens.title: Scene view navigation controls
screens.narratorSegment: Learning navigation controls is like learning to drive a vehicle: muscle memory makes everything feel natural. In the Scene view you combine mouse buttons with keyboard keys for efficient movement. Hold the right mouse button and use W, A, S, D to fly forward, left, back, and right. Use Q and E while holding the right mouse button to move the camera vertically. To orbit around a selected object, hold the Alt key and drag with the left mouse button; this keeps the selected object at the center of your rotation and is essential when you need to inspect details. The mouse scroll wheel zooms the view in and out smoothly, which is useful for fine adjustments or getting an overall view. Practice these motions together: first hold right mouse and press W for a few seconds, then use A/D strafing, and finish with Alt + left-drag around a selected object. A common misconception is thinking Scene navigation affects gameplay; it only moves your editor camera. Always verify object transforms in the Inspector rather than relying solely on approximate mouse movements. As an example, move toward a cube using W, orbit around it with Alt and left-drag, then check the cube's Transform X, Y, Z in the Inspector to confirm exact placement. This combination of visual navigation and numeric confirmation is a reliable workflow.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Process Flow
Navigation steps
Follow these numbered steps until they become second nature.
1
Fly: Right-click + W/A/S/D
Hold right mouse and move around like a free camera: W forward, A left, S back, D right.
2
Vertical motion: Q / E
While holding right mouse, press Q to move down and E to move up to change elevation smoothly.
3
Orbit: Alt + Left-drag
Hold Alt and drag with left mouse to rotate around a selected object—great for close inspection.
4
Zoom: Mouse scroll wheel
Scroll to zoom in and out; combine with orbit and fly for precise control.
Key Takeaway

Practice these controls in sequence: fly, vertical adjust, orbit, and zoom. Use numeric values in the Inspector to confirm accuracy.

Practice drill
Try this loop: hold right mouse and press W for three seconds, strafe left with A, move up with E, then Alt + left-drag to orbit a selected cube, and finally scroll in to inspect a face.
Concrete example
Select the Main Camera in Hierarchy. Hold right mouse and press W to fly closer, then Alt + left-drag to orbit around the camera to see its view frustum in the Scene.
Misconception
Some learners assume these controls change object transforms directly. They move the editor camera. Use the Inspector or transform tools to change object properties persistently.

screens.title: Create and manipulate a Cube
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through creating and editing a simple GameObject: a cube. This exercise establishes the basic loop you'll use repeatedly. First, in the Hierarchy window right-click and choose 3D Object > Cube. The cube appears in the Scene view and is added to the Hierarchy. Select it and look to the Inspector: you'll find Transform fields for Position, Rotation, and Scale. Use the Move tool (W key) to drag the cube around in the Scene until it rests above the plane. Use the Rotate tool (E key) to change its orientation and the Scale tool (R key) to resize it. As you move the object, watch the numeric values in the Inspector update; this is important for precise placement and for copying values across objects. After arranging the cube, press Ctrl+S (or Cmd+S on Mac) to save the scene; save it under Assets/Scenes as MyFirstScene. A typical beginner error is moving objects visually without saving, then losing work when Unity or the editor state changes. This simple create-and-save loop—create, place, inspect, save—builds a reliable habit for all future editing.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Hands-on Activity
Create a Cube — step sequence
Follow these steps to create, modify, and save your first scene object.
1
Right-click in Hierarchy > 3D Object > Cube. It appears in Scene and Hierarchy.
2
Select the Cube and use the Move tool (W) to reposition it. Watch the Transform fields in the Inspector update numerically.
3
Use Rotate (E) and Scale (R) to adjust orientation and size. Use exact numbers in the Inspector when precision matters.
4
Save Scene: File > Save Scene As... save to Assets/Scenes/MyFirstScene, then File > Save Project.
Example
Create Cube, set Position Y to 1.0 in the Inspector so it sits above the ground. Set Scale X to 2 to make it wider. These numeric edits ensure repeatable results across scenes.
Common mistake
Relying only on mouse drag without checking the Inspector can produce inconsistent placements. Use numeric values for precise alignment.
Key Takeaway

Create, inspect numeric values, adjust tools, and save. That sequence protects your work and makes it reproducible.

screens.title: Scene view vs Game view
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between Scene and Game views is essential. The Scene view is an editor camera used for composing and arranging GameObjects—it's flexible and can be moved freely so you can place objects and adjust lighting. The Game view, in contrast, renders the active Camera's output and shows what your player will actually see at runtime. Use Scene while you build: place objects, set up lighting, and organize Hierarchy. Use Game to preview gameplay, camera framing, and visual fidelity. A useful practice is frequent context checks: after placing or adjusting objects in the Scene, press Play or switch to Game view to see if the changes look correct from the player's perspective. A common misconception is believing placement that looks good in Scene will automatically look correct in Game; camera position, field of view, and UI overlays often change that appearance. For example, you might place a tree that looks well-framed in Scene but appears out of frame in the Game view because the active camera is positioned differently. The reliable workflow is edit in Scene, then test in Game, adjust in Scene guided by Game feedback, and repeat until the visual result matches your intention.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Comparison
Scene view
Use this for building, placing, and arranging objects with free camera control.
  • Interactive editing camera with free movement.
  • Good for object placement and scene composition.
  • Does not show runtime camera effects or UI overlays.
Concrete example
Place a light and move it visually until a character's face looks lit. Then switch to Game to confirm the lighting from the player's camera.
Game view
Use this to preview exactly what the player will see from the active camera.
  • Renders active camera, post-processing, and UI overlays.
  • Use to validate framing, gameplay visibility, and visual effects.
  • Switch between Scene and Game frequently to iterate.
Key Takeaway
Design in Scene; verify in Game. Iteration between the two ensures what you build matches the player's experience.

screens.title: Hierarchy and GameObject relationships
screens.narratorSegment: The Hierarchy window shows every GameObject in the active scene and reveals parent-child relationships that matter for movement and organization. A GameObject may contain child objects; when you move the parent, the children follow. This is useful for grouping parts of a complex object—imagine a car GameObject with wheel GameObjects as children: rotating the car rotates its wheels with it. Grouping also simplifies transform editing and helps keep the scene tidy. When you create a new object in the Hierarchy it inherits local transform relationships relative to its parent. Misunderstandings often arise around where to place scripts and components: adding a movement script to a parent moves the whole group, while adding it to a child moves only that child. A practical example: group a lamp and its bulb under a single GameObject so you can toggle the lamp on and off by enabling or disabling the parent. Use clear naming and folder-like grouping to avoid confusion as scenes grow. Finally, remember that the Project window stores assets, while the Hierarchy lists instances of those assets present in the current scene. This separation keeps your project scalable and makes it easy to reuse assets across scenes.

keyIdea.text: Parent-child relationships let you move and control groups of objects together. Name and group objects to keep scenes maintainable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Definition
Hierarchy concepts
Understand how parent-child relationships affect transforms and scene organization.
Parent follows: Moving a parent GameObject moves its children too, which is useful for grouping parts of a larger object.
Local vs global: Children have local transform values relative to their parent; global position is computed by combining transforms.
Component placement: Attach scripts to the object responsible for the behavior you want—parent-level scripts affect all children.
Concrete example
Make a Car parent object and add Wheel children. Rotate the Car to steer all wheels at once. Add a script to the Car parent to control the movement of the entire vehicle.
Best practices
  • Use clear naming for parents and children.
  • Create empty parent holders for logical grouping.
  • Keep reusable prefabs in Project and instances in Hierarchy.
Common mistake
Accidentally parenting unrelated objects can cause unexpected transforms. Check the Hierarchy before moving or deleting parent objects.

screens.title: Inspector and component editing
screens.narratorSegment: The Inspector is where you change the details of a selected object. Anything you select—an object in the Hierarchy or an asset in the Project—shows properties and components in the Inspector. Transform fields for Position, Rotation, and Scale are fundamental: they accept numeric input for precise placement. Many components expose fields for materials, physics, and script variables, so you can tune behavior without opening code. A practical habit is to use the Inspector for final numeric adjustments after moving something visually in the Scene. For example, if you nudge an object near the origin, open the Inspector and set Position X, Y, Z to 0, 1, 0 respectively to snap it into place. A common misconception is thinking the Inspector only shows readouts; it is the primary place to change values permanently. If you're using a script with public fields, expose and edit those values here to test parameters quickly without recompiling code. This speeds iteration and keeps experiments isolated to editable components. Inspector and component editing means use the inspector to confirm and set exact transform and component values. it is the authoritative place for object configuration.. In practical terms, adjusting transforms and component values with precision. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Tooling
Inspector workflow
Use the Inspector to set exact values and tune components without code changes.
Numeric confirmation
After positioning visually, set Position X/Y/Z in the Inspector to precise values so placement is reproducible across sessions.
Script variables
If a script exposes public fields, you can adjust them here at edit time to test behaviors without recompiling.

screens.title: Saving scenes and projects

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Process
Save workflow
Follow these steps to keep your scene and project safe and organized.
1. Create an Assets/Scenes folder in the Project window if it doesn't exist.
2. File > Save Scene As... name it descriptive (example: MyFirstScene) and save into Assets/Scenes.
3. Use Ctrl+S or Cmd+S as a fast save shortcut while editing.
4. After asset or setting changes, choose File > Save Project to persist those project-level changes.
Key Takeaway

Saving is habitual: scenes are files in Assets, and saving the project commits assets and settings. Do both to avoid lost work.

Example
After positioning your cube, press Ctrl+S and save as Assets/Scenes/MyFirstScene, then File > Save Project so the asset references are preserved.
Mistake
Saving only the scene but not the project can leave imported assets or settings unsaved. Save both to be safe.

screens.title: Customize and save your Editor layout
screens.narratorSegment: Customizing your Editor layout tailors the workspace to your workflow and reduces friction. You can drag and dock windows: for example, move the Game view next to the Scene view to compare edits and preview quickly. Once you have a layout that feels productive, save it under Window > Layouts > Save Layout and give it a name, so you can recall it on any project or after closing Unity. Personal layouts are useful when you focus on specific tasks—level design might favor a larger Scene view while UI work favors Game plus Inspector. A common beginner mistake is to stick with the default layout even when it slows you down; small changes can improve speed. Another tip: if the layout becomes confusing, reset to default via Window > Layouts > Default, then adjust incrementally. Concrete practice: arrange the windows as you prefer, then save the new layout as MyCustomLayout. This small step means your preferred arrangement is always available and reproducible across sessions. Customize layout

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn how the Unity Editor is organized and why each window matters for building games. The editor is more than a single view: it's a collection of specialized windows—Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector—that together form your workspace. Think of the Scene view as your 3D workshop where you place and arrange objects, the Game view as a preview of what players will see, the Hierarchy as the scene's table of contents, the Project window as the project's asset library, and the Inspector as the detailed settings panel for whatever you select. We will also practice navigation controls used to fly and orbit through 3D space and cover the basics of creating, saving, and organizing scenes. Mastery of these tools speeds up every task that follows, whether you are placing a cube, positioning a camera, or building a level. A common beginner mistake is to ignore the Project organization and Inspector details; this leads to confusion as a project grows. As you listen, imagine creating a new project, placing a cube, and saving a scene. Keep an eye out for the practical checks and a small hands-on activity that shows how these pieces connect. By the end you'll have a clear mental map of the editor and a small routine to keep your work safe and organized.

These learning objectives are skills you will practice and verify during the lesson. First, you'll be able to identify the purpose of key windows: Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector. That means you can explain when to use each window and locate the controls you need. Second, you'll master basic Scene view navigation using mouse and keyboard shortcuts such as holding the right mouse button with W, A, S, D movement, Q and E vertical movement, Alt plus left drag for orbiting, and the scroll wheel for zoom. You will practice these until they feel natural. Third, you'll create, save, and load Unity scenes and projects, using File menus and the common shortcut to save a scene. Saving often prevents lost work and is a habit every developer should keep. Fourth, you'll learn how to customize and save your Editor layout so your most-used windows are where you expect them. Custom layouts save time and reduce friction as projects grow. Each objective includes short practice tasks so you can confirm competency and build muscle memory.

This screen connects objectives to short, verifiable practices you can do immediately. For window identification, open the default scene and click each major window: notice how selecting a GameObject updates the Inspector, and how the Project window contains files even if they aren’t in the current scene. For navigation, practice the movement pattern: hold the right mouse button, press W to move forward, A to strafe left, S backward, D right, Q and E to move vertically, and use Alt plus left-drag to orbit a selected object while using scroll wheel to zoom. For saving, create a new Cube, then go to File and Save Scene As, save inside Assets/Scenes as MyFirstScene, and finally choose File Save Project. For layout customization, drag the Game view next to the Scene view, then go to Window, Layouts, Save Layout and name it. These short tasks build muscle memory and create artifacts—saved scenes and a custom layout—you can point to as proof of competency.

The Unity Editor is an integrated development environment composed of several specialized windows that each play a unique role in building a game. The Scene view is your interactive 3D canvas where you place, move, and arrange GameObjects such as characters, lights, and props. The Game view shows the rendered output from the active camera and simulates what a player will see during runtime. The Hierarchy lists every GameObject in the current scene and reveals parent-child relationships you can use to group and transform objects together. The Project window is your project's asset repository: models, textures, audio, scripts, and saved scenes live here whether or not they are in the current scene. Finally, the Inspector displays editable properties and components for whatever you have selected, giving you precise control over transform values, material settings, and script variables. A helpful way to remember their roles is to treat the Project as your toolbox, the Hierarchy as the parts list for this scene, the Scene as the assembly table, the Inspector as the fine-tuner, and the Game view as the test bench. A common misconception is to confuse Scene and Game: editing happens in Scene, while Game shows runtime output. Practice by selecting a default cube, noticing how the Inspector updates, and dragging an asset from the Project into the Scene so it appears in the Hierarchy. That small loop demonstrates how the windows interact and why understanding them speeds every stage of development.

Learning navigation controls is like learning to drive a vehicle: muscle memory makes everything feel natural. In the Scene view you combine mouse buttons with keyboard keys for efficient movement. Hold the right mouse button and use W, A, S, D to fly forward, left, back, and right. Use Q and E while holding the right mouse button to move the camera vertically. To orbit around a selected object, hold the Alt key and drag with the left mouse button; this keeps the selected object at the center of your rotation and is essential when you need to inspect details. The mouse scroll wheel zooms the view in and out smoothly, which is useful for fine adjustments or getting an overall view. Practice these motions together: first hold right mouse and press W for a few seconds, then use A/D strafing, and finish with Alt + left-drag around a selected object. A common misconception is thinking Scene navigation affects gameplay; it only moves your editor camera. Always verify object transforms in the Inspector rather than relying solely on approximate mouse movements. As an example, move toward a cube using W, orbit around it with Alt and left-drag, then check the cube's Transform X, Y, Z in the Inspector to confirm exact placement. This combination of visual navigation and numeric confirmation is a reliable workflow.

Now we'll walk through creating and editing a simple GameObject: a cube. This exercise establishes the basic loop you'll use repeatedly. First, in the Hierarchy window right-click and choose 3D Object > Cube. The cube appears in the Scene view and is added to the Hierarchy. Select it and look to the Inspector: you'll find Transform fields for Position, Rotation, and Scale. Use the Move tool (W key) to drag the cube around in the Scene until it rests above the plane. Use the Rotate tool (E key) to change its orientation and the Scale tool (R key) to resize it. As you move the object, watch the numeric values in the Inspector update; this is important for precise placement and for copying values across objects. After arranging the cube, press Ctrl+S (or Cmd+S on Mac) to save the scene; save it under Assets/Scenes as MyFirstScene. A typical beginner error is moving objects visually without saving, then losing work when Unity or the editor state changes. This simple create-and-save loop—create, place, inspect, save—builds a reliable habit for all future editing.

Understanding the difference between Scene and Game views is essential. The Scene view is an editor camera used for composing and arranging GameObjects—it's flexible and can be moved freely so you can place objects and adjust lighting. The Game view, in contrast, renders the active Camera's output and shows what your player will actually see at runtime. Use Scene while you build: place objects, set up lighting, and organize Hierarchy. Use Game to preview gameplay, camera framing, and visual fidelity. A useful practice is frequent context checks: after placing or adjusting objects in the Scene, press Play or switch to Game view to see if the changes look correct from the player's perspective. A common misconception is believing placement that looks good in Scene will automatically look correct in Game; camera position, field of view, and UI overlays often change that appearance. For example, you might place a tree that looks well-framed in Scene but appears out of frame in the Game view because the active camera is positioned differently. The reliable workflow is edit in Scene, then test in Game, adjust in Scene guided by Game feedback, and repeat until the visual result matches your intention.

The Hierarchy window shows every GameObject in the active scene and reveals parent-child relationships that matter for movement and organization. A GameObject may contain child objects; when you move the parent, the children follow. This is useful for grouping parts of a complex object—imagine a car GameObject with wheel GameObjects as children: rotating the car rotates its wheels with it. Grouping also simplifies transform editing and helps keep the scene tidy. When you create a new object in the Hierarchy it inherits local transform relationships relative to its parent. Misunderstandings often arise around where to place scripts and components: adding a movement script to a parent moves the whole group, while adding it to a child moves only that child. A practical example: group a lamp and its bulb under a single GameObject so you can toggle the lamp on and off by enabling or disabling the parent. Use clear naming and folder-like grouping to avoid confusion as scenes grow. Finally, remember that the Project window stores assets, while the Hierarchy lists instances of those assets present in the current scene. This separation keeps your project scalable and makes it easy to reuse assets across scenes.

The Inspector is where you change the details of a selected object. Anything you select—an object in the Hierarchy or an asset in the Project—shows properties and components in the Inspector. Transform fields for Position, Rotation, and Scale are fundamental: they accept numeric input for precise placement. Many components expose fields for materials, physics, and script variables, so you can tune behavior without opening code. A practical habit is to use the Inspector for final numeric adjustments after moving something visually in the Scene. For example, if you nudge an object near the origin, open the Inspector and set Position X, Y, Z to 0, 1, 0 respectively to snap it into place. A common misconception is thinking the Inspector only shows readouts; it is the primary place to change values permanently. If you're using a script with public fields, expose and edit those values here to test parameters quickly without recompiling code. This speeds iteration and keeps experiments isolated to editable components.
